routes.label: Find the base using the strip's perpendicular width

question:
Two strips of width \(1\) overlap at an angle of \(\alpha\) as shown. The area of the overlap (shown shaded) is

[Figure 1](figures/1989_AMC_12_Q13_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Each strip is bounded by two parallel lines, so their overlap is a parallelogram. Choose its horizontal bottom side as the base, and call its length \(b\). The corresponding height is the horizontal strip's width, \(1\), so the area is \(b\).

To find \(b\), call the left and right endpoints of this base \(P\) and \(Q\). Draw a perpendicular from \(P\) to the slanted boundary through \(Q\), meeting it at \(T\). The slanted strip has perpendicular width \(1\), so \(PT=1\).

The marked angle \(\alpha\) is obtuse. Set \(\beta=180^\circ-\alpha\), the acute angle \(PQT\). In right triangle \(PQT\), the hypotenuse is \(PQ=b\), so
\[
\sin\beta=\frac{PT}{PQ}=\frac1b.
\]
Supplementary angles have equal sines, hence \(\sin\beta=\sin\alpha\), giving
\[
\text{Area}=b\cdot1=\frac1{\sin\alpha}.
\]
The crossing strips give \(0<\alpha<180^\circ\), so \(\sin\alpha>0\) and division is valid. The answer is \(\boxed{\frac1{\sin\alpha}}\), choice \(\text{B}\).

edges.reason: The target finds a scalar difference from 90 or 180 and distinguishes the two sum relations. It does not require the broader geometric angle-composition/bisector repertoire; Gemini conflates elementary subtraction of measures with that whole procedure.
edges.scope: Angle-composition and bisection experience supporting complements and supplements

edges.reason: Point-to-point shortest-distance language is a helpful model, but perpendicular-shortest distance is a separate fact and not derived merely from the two-point line axiom.
The distance in question is the length of the perpendicular from the point, so perpendicularity identifies which segment is measured.
Angle-independent ratios use proportional sides of similar right triangles.
Quadrant signs help remember the identities. Reflecting (cos(alpha),sin(alpha)) to (-cos(alpha),sin(alpha)) proves the supplementary identities directly without a quadrant-sign table.
edges.scope: Tracking signs in supplementary and related-angle identities

edges.reason: Parallelograms and trapezoids are defined through how many pairs of opposite sides are parallel, using parallel-line meaning.
edges.scope: defining parallelograms and trapezoids by parallel sides

edges.reason: The target must identify the base and corresponding height of a parallelogram, not merely multiply two labeled numbers. This uses the pair of parallel opposite sides that defines that shape and locates the opposite line. Restrict necessity to that meaning, without requiring all trapezoid properties or a rectangle derivation.
edges.scope: The parallelogram opposite-side meaning when identifying a base and its corresponding perpendicular height
